name: Apollo 16 science station
intro: John Young and Charlie Duke set up this nuclear-powered science station near Orion in April 1972. One instrument was ruined on day one when a cable was torn loose, but the seismometer kept listening for moonquakes until NASA ended support for the stations in 1977.

hotspots.title: The torn cable
hotspots.text: While working, John Young caught his foot on the heat-flow experiment’s cable and tore it out of the central station. That instrument never sent back any data.

photo.alt: A foil-wrapped box on the grey ground with a loose ribbon cable coiled near its base.
photo.caption: The torn heat-flow cable lying coiled at the back of the central station.
photo.licenseEvidence: Apollo Lunar Surface Journal image library: NASA Hasselblad frame AS16-113-18348, NASA film scan (not a third-party restoration). NASA: images and video "generally are not subject to copyright in the United States" (https://www.nasa.gov/nasa-brand-center/images-and-media/).

hotspots.title: The central station
hotspots.text: The station’s brain and radio. In September 1977 NASA stopped collecting its data and switched the experiments off. Scout’s check: its seismometer was still working at the end.

photo.alt: A seismometer under a silver blanket in front of a foil-covered box and a finned generator.
photo.caption: The seismometer in front, with the central station and the finned generator behind.
photo.licenseEvidence: NASA Image and Video Library item as16-113-18347 (JSC); no third-party credit or copyright notice on the item. NASA: images and video "generally are not subject to copyright in the United States" (https://www.nasa.gov/nasa-brand-center/images-and-media/).

hotspots.title: The seismometer
hotspots.text: Under a silver blanket, the seismometer made the Apollo network four stations strong. Together they recorded thousands of moonquakes and meteorite hits.

hotspots.title: Grenade launcher
hotspots.text: This mortar box fired grenades by radio after the crew left. Grenades 2, 4 and 3 flew, then a tilt sensor failed and grenade 1 was never launched.

hotspots.title: The nuclear generator
hotspots.text: This black-finned can turned heat from plutonium into electricity, so the station worked day and night.

funFact: Three of its four rocket-fired grenades were launched by radio after the crew left, to make small moonquakes; the fourth never fired.
whyLeft: It was meant to stay and work for years, and most of it did, until NASA stopped supporting the Apollo stations in 1977.
repurpose: The torn heat-flow cable could in theory be spliced, but after 50 years in the dust the safest use is as a test of how long Moon equipment survives.
